usage: 고속 (high speed) + 도로 = the big inter-city expressway
fixed traffic phrase; 막히다 (be blocked) is intransitive, so use 가/이 not 을/를
공사 工事 = construction work; the sign you see when a lane is closed
go by this road / take this road
route-marking 로/으로, not 에서; tells which road you travel along
examples: 이 도로는 넓어요.
This road is wide.
simplest description; 넓다 (wide) takes the subject with 은/는 here
출근 시간이라 도로가 많이 막혀요.
It's rush hour, so the road is really jammed.
everyday complaint; 막히다 stays intransitive, so 도로'가' not 도로'를'
내비가 이 도로로 가라고 했어요.
The GPS told me to take this road.
real driving situation; route particle 로 + indirect command 가라고 하다
nuance: 도로 道路 (道 way + 路 path) is the neutral, infrastructure word for a paved road that cars drive on — what an engineer or a traffic report means by 'road'. The sharp contrast is with 거리: 도로 stresses the vehicle surface (도로가 막히다, 도로 공사), while 거리 is a shopping/walking street you stroll down; you would never say 거리가 막히다 about car traffic. It is also broader than 골목(길) (a narrow alley) and 차도 (the car-only carriageway as opposed to 인도, the sidewalk). Register is plain and works everywhere from signs to news. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle when you mean a route: 'go by this road' is 이 도로'로' 가요 (route-marking 로/으로), not 도로'에서' 가요, because 에서 marks where an action happens, while 로 marks the path you move along.

Using 도로 for a lively shopping street: a street you walk and browse is 거리 (e.g. 가로수길 같은 거리), whereas 도로 sounds like an asphalt traffic artery.
Marking the route with 에서: to express 'let's take this road' say 이 도로'로' 가요, not 이 도로에서 가요 (에서 would mean an action performed on the road).

usage: destination 에 + 가다; 주유소 is a place you head to
the verb is 넣다 (put in); the object is 기름 (oil/fuel), not 주유소
셀프 (self) + 주유소; you pump it yourself, very common in Korea
기름값 = fuel price; describe the station's prices, not the station 'being cheap'
examples: 근처에 주유소가 있어요?
Is there a gas station nearby?
simple existence question; 있다 takes the subject with 가
주유소에서 기름을 가득 넣었어요.
I filled the tank all the way up at the gas station.
everyday refueling; 에서 marks where the action happens, 가득 = full
셀프 주유소라서 직접 넣어야 해요.
It's a self-service station, so you have to pump it yourself.
real situation; -아야 하다 (have to) + 직접 (in person/oneself)
nuance: 주유소 注油所 literally stacks 注 (pour) + 油 (oil) + 所 (place) = 'a place where you pour oil', i.e. a fuel station. Because the 油 is 'oil/fuel', Koreans say 기름(을) 넣다 ('put in oil') even for gasoline — 기름 covers gasoline, diesel, everything in the tank. The natural verb is 넣다 (put in), so the object is 기름, never the station itself. As a 소(所) place-noun it behaves like other locations: 에 for going there (주유소에 가요), 에서 for the action done there (주유소에서 넣어요). The big English-speaker pitfall is importing 'gas': do not say 가스 — 가스 in Korean means cooking/LPG gas, and a fuel stop is 주유소. A second trap is making the station the grammatical object: you fill the car with 기름, so it's 기름을 넣다, not 주유소를 넣다.

Saying 주유소를 넣어요 — the thing you put in is fuel, so it must be 주유소'에서' 기름'을' 넣어요.
Saying 주유소가 싸요 to mean fuel is cheap — describe the price: 그 주유소는 기름값이 싸요 (its gas price is cheap).

usage: 창가 (window side) + 좌석; opposite is 통로 좌석 (aisle seat)
번호 番號 = number; the figure printed on your ticket
예약하다 (book in advance); 좌석 is the object with 을
등급 = class (e.g. 일반실/특실 on the KTX)
examples: 제 좌석은 어디예요?
Where is my seat?
simple question on a train or plane; 은/는 marks 'my seat' as topic
창가 좌석으로 주세요.
A window seat, please.
everyday booking line; 으로 = 'as/in the form of', i.e. choosing among options
예매한 좌석에 다른 사람이 앉아 있었어요.
Someone else was sitting in the seat I'd reserved.
real-trip trouble; 예매하다 (book a ticket) + 에 앉다 (sit in/at)
nuance: 좌석 座席 (座 a seat + 席 a mat/place) is the formal, ticketed word for a numbered seat on a bus, train, plane, or in a theater. Its everyday near-synonym is 자리, and the dividing line is register and specificity: 자리 is the casual catch-all ('a spot/place to sit', also 'a vacant spot'), while 좌석 is what appears on tickets, signboards, and reservation screens — you reserve a 좌석, but you save someone a 자리. Natural partners are 창가/통로 좌석 (window/aisle), 좌석 번호, 좌석 예약. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: first, pick the verb by the surface — you 앉다 'on/at' a seat with 에 (좌석에 앉다), not 좌석을 앉다; second, watch the spelling, since 자석 (磁石) means 'magnet' and 좌석 is the seat — the ㅗ vs ㅏ vowel is the whole difference.

mistakes: Using 좌석 in casual chat where 자리 fits — for 'save me a spot' say 자리 좀 맡아 줘, not 좌석; 좌석 sounds like a booked transport seat.
Saying 좌석을 앉아요 — you sit at a seat: 좌석'에' 앉아요 (place particle 에).
Misspelling it 자석 — that is 磁石 'magnet'; the seat is 좌석 with the ㅗ vowel.

usage: goal-marking 에 + 도착하다; 에 is required, never 를
최종 最終 (final) + 목적지; the last stop when you have transfers
입력하다 (input) into a GPS; here 목적지 is the object with 를
all the way to the destination
까지 = up to/as far as; marks the end point of the route
examples: 목적지가 어디예요?
Where are you headed?
simple; a taxi driver's opening question, subject marked with 가
목적지까지 한 시간쯤 걸려요.
It takes about an hour to the destination.
everyday travel time; 까지 (up to) + 걸리다 (take time)
내비게이션에 목적지를 입력했어요.
I entered the destination into the GPS.
real driving step; here 목적지 is the object you type in, so 를
nuance: 목적지 目的地 stacks 目 (eye/aim) + 的 (target) + 地 (place/ground) = 'the targeted place', the spot you are traveling toward. The instructive contrast is with 도착지 and 출발지: 목적지 highlights intention ('where I aim to go'), 도착지 is the neutral 'arrival point', and its true opposite is 출발지 (departure point) — pairing 목적지 with 출발지 is the standard map/app framing. Do not confuse 목적지 (place) with 목적 alone (目的 = a purpose/aim, abstract), nor with 목표 (a goal you strive for). It is a slightly formal travel word used by taxi drivers and navigation apps. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you arrive 'at' it with 에 — 목적지'에' 도착하다 — never 목적지를 도착하다, because 도착하다 is intransitive; but when you type it into a GPS the verb is transitive, so it flips to 목적지'를' 입력하다.

mistakes: Saying 목적지를 도착해요 — 도착하다 (to arrive) is intransitive and needs the goal particle: 목적지'에' 도착해요.
Confusing 목적지 (the place) with 목적 (the purpose) — 'my destination is Busan' is 목적지는 부산이에요, not 목적은 부산이에요 (that would mean 'my purpose is Busan').
Using 목적지 for a starting point — that is 출발지; 목적지 is only the place you are going to.

usage: 거리 + 를 + 걷다; the path you walk takes 를 here
복잡하다 (complicated/crowded) describing foot traffic and bustle
공연 公演 = performance; the kind done on a pedestrian street
there are many people on the street
location 에 + 있다-type existence; pedestrians, not cars
examples: 이 거리는 사람이 많아요.
This street is busy with people.
simple description; topic 은/는 on the street, 많다 about people
주말이라 거리가 사람들로 복잡해요.
It's the weekend, so the street is packed with people.
everyday scene; 로 = 'with (filled by)' + 복잡하다 (crowded)
거리에서 버스킹 공연을 봤어요.
I watched a busking performance on the street.
real outing; 에서 marks where the watching happened
nuance: 거리 (street) is a native Korean word — note it is NOT the Sino-Korean 距離 'distance', even though the two are spelled and written identically and are told apart only by context. As 'street' it means a public way lined with shops, cafes, and pedestrians that you stroll and browse (think 명동 거리, 가로수길). The sharp contrast is with 도로 道路: 거리 centers on people and street life (거리 공연, 거리가 복잡하다), while 도로 centers on the car surface (도로가 막히다) — Koreans say 도로가 막히다 for a traffic jam but never 거리가 막히다 in that sense. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this homonym: 'the distance is far' is 거리가 멀다, but 'the street is busy' is 거리가 복잡하다 — same word, and only the predicate and situation tell you whether someone means a road you walk or a span you measure.

Saying 거리를 걸어가요 vs 거리에서 — to 'walk along' the street the path can take 를 (거리를 걷다); 에서 is for an action located on the street (거리에서 공연을 보다).

usage: 에서 + 기다리다; the place where the waiting happens
number + 번 (counter) + 승강장; matches station signage
direction 으로 + 가다; head toward the platform
안전선 安全線 = safety line; '승강장 안전선 안쪽으로' is the classic announcement
examples: 승강장에서 기차를 기다려요.
I'm waiting for the train on the platform.
simple; 에서 marks the location of waiting
3번 승강장으로 가세요.
Please go to platform 3.
everyday direction; 으로 (toward) + 가세요 (polite go)
승강장 안전선 안쪽으로 물러나 주세요.
Please step back behind the platform safety line.
real announcement you'll actually hear; 안쪽으로 (toward the inside) + 물러나다 (step back)
nuance: 승강장 乘降場 stacks 乘 (board/get on) + 降 (alight/get off) + 場 (place/field) = 'the place where you board and get off', i.e. the platform along the tracks. It is the formal term on signage and in announcements; the everyday spoken equivalent is 플랫폼 (the English loanword), and 타는 곳 ('boarding place') is the plain-Korean label posted in many stations — all three point to the same spot. The crucial contrast is with 정류장 停留場 (a bus/tram STOP at the roadside) and 역 (the whole STATION building): the 승강장 is the specific edge where you stand beside the train, inside the 역. As a 場 place-noun it takes 에서 for waiting (승강장에서 기다려요) and 으로 for moving toward it (승강장으로 가요). The English-speaker pitfall is treating the platform as something you wait 'for': you wait for the TRAIN on the platform, so it's 승강장에서 기차를 기다려요, never 승강장을 기다려요.

Mixing up 승강장 with 정류장 — 승강장 is the train/subway platform inside a station, while 정류장 is a roadside bus stop.
Confusing 승강장 with 역 — 역 is the entire station; the 승강장 is only the boarding strip beside the tracks.

usage: the verb is 매다 (to tie/fasten), as with a tie or belt
풀다 (to loosen/undo); the natural opposite of 매다
착용 着用 = wearing/putting on; the formal word on signs and laws
if you don't wear a seatbelt
negation 안 + 매다 + 면 (if); used for warnings and fines
examples: 안전벨트를 매세요.
Please fasten your seatbelt.
simple polite command; the standard taxi/airplane line
차가 출발하기 전에 안전벨트를 꼭 매요.
I always buckle up before the car starts moving.
everyday habit; -기 전에 (before) + 꼭 (without fail)
신호 대기 중이니까 잠깐 안전벨트를 풀어도 돼요.
We're stopped at the light, so you can unbuckle for a sec.
real moment; -아도 되다 (it's okay to) + 풀다 (undo)
nuance: 안전벨트 is a hybrid: Sino-Korean 안전 安全 (安 peace/safe + 全 complete) = 'safety' + the loanword 벨트 (belt) — so literally a 'safety belt'. A common everyday synonym is just 벨트 ('안전벨트 매', often shortened to '벨트 매'), and on signs/laws you meet 착용 (着用 'wearing'). The make-or-break point is the verb: Korean fastens a belt with 매다 (to tie/fasten, the same verb as a necktie) and undoes it with 풀다 (to loosen) — NOT 입다/벗다, which are for clothing you put on the body. That is the central English-speaker pitfall: English 'wear/put on a seatbelt' tempts learners toward 입다, but 안전벨트를 입다 is wrong; it must be 안전벨트를 매다. Likewise 'take it off' is 풀다 (undo), not 벗다 (which is for shoes/clothes/hats).

usage: head-gear verb 쓰다 (wear on the head), same as a hat/glasses
벗다 (take off); the opposite of 쓰다 for head items
자전거 (bicycle) + 헬멧; also 오토바이 헬멧 for motorcycles
착용 着用 (wearing) + 의무 義務 (duty); legal phrasing for kickboards/bikes
examples: 자전거 탈 때 헬멧을 써요.
I wear a helmet when I ride a bike.
simple habit; -ㄹ 때 (when) + 쓰다 for head gear
킥보드 탈 때도 헬멧을 꼭 써야 해요.
You have to wear a helmet on a kickboard too.
everyday rule; 꼭 (definitely) + -아야 하다 (must)
헬멧이 좀 작아서 머리가 꽉 껴요.
The helmet's a bit small, so it squeezes my head.
real fitting issue; 꽉 (tightly) + 끼다 (be wedged/snug)
nuance: 헬멧 is a straight loanword from English 'helmet', with no hanja, used for the protective head shell worn on bikes, motorcycles, and especially 전동킥보드 (electric kickboards). A close native-ish synonym is 안전모 安全帽 (安全 safety + 帽 hat/cap), but 안전모 leans toward construction/industrial hard hats, while 헬멧 is the everyday sports/riding word — both can appear in safety rules. The decisive grammar point is the verb family for things worn on the HEAD: Korean uses 쓰다 to put on a helmet, hat, or glasses, and 벗다 to take them off. This is the key English-speaker pitfall — 'wear a helmet' invites 입다 (clothing) or even 풀다 (undo, from belts), but neither fits: it must be 헬멧을 쓰다 and 헬멧을 벗다. Note 쓰다 is a busy homonym (also 'to write', 'to use', 'to be bitter'), so context, not the verb alone, tells you it means 'wear on the head' here.

The decisive grammar point is the verb family for things worn on the HEAD: Korean uses 쓰다 to put on a helmet, hat, or glasses, and 벗다 to take them off. Note 쓰다 is a busy homonym (also 'to write', 'to use', 'to be bitter'), so context, not the verb alone, tells you it means 'wear on the head' here.
A close native-ish synonym is 안전모 安全帽 (安全 safety + 帽 hat/cap), but 안전모 leans toward construction/industrial hard hats, while 헬멧 is the everyday sports/riding word — both can appear in safety rules.
헬멧 is a straight loanword from English 'helmet', with no hanja.
'Wear a helmet' invites 입다 (clothing) or even 풀다 (undo, from belts), but neither fits: it must be 헬멧을 쓰다 and 헬멧을 벗다.

mistakes: Saying 헬멧을 입다 — 입다 is for body clothing; head gear uses 헬멧을 '쓰다'.
Saying 헬멧을 풀다 to remove it — 풀다 is for undoing belts/knots; take off head gear with 헬멧을 '벗다'.
Assuming 안전모 and 헬멧 are interchangeable — 안전모 sounds like an industrial hard hat, while a riding/cycling helmet is 헬멧.

usage: 에서 + 타다; the action of getting on happens there
the natural pair; 과/와 links the two endpoints
출발 出發 + 시각 時刻 (point in time); the time on your ticket
examples: 출발역이 서울역이에요.
The departure station is Seoul Station.
simple identity sentence; 이에요 (it is)
출발역에서 미리 표를 받았어요.
I picked up the ticket in advance at the departure station.
everyday step; 미리 (beforehand) + 에서 for the place of the action
출발역을 잘못 알아서 다른 역으로 갔어요.
I had the wrong departure station, so I went to a different one.
real mistake; here 출발역 is the object of 알다 (know), so it takes 을
nuance: 출발역 出發驛 stacks 出 (go out) + 發 (set off/emit) + 驛 (station) = 'the station you set off from', the origin of a train trip. Its built-in opposite is 도착역 (arrival station, 到着驛), and the two are the standard pair on tickets and booking screens. Note the difference between 출발역 (the origin STATION) and 출발 (出發, the act of departing) and 출발지 (a more general 'departure point', not necessarily a rail station): for trains and subways you want 출발역. Register is plain and travel-flavored. The English-speaker pitfall is the boarding particle: you get on a train AT the station, so it's 출발역'에서' 타다 (action-location 에서), never 출발역을 타다 — 타다 takes the vehicle as its object (기차를 타다), while the station is just where that happens.

structuredNuance.t: 출발역 means 'the station you set off from', the origin of a train trip. Register is plain and travel-flavored.

出發驛 stacks 出 (go out) + 發 (set off/emit) + 驛 (station) = 'the station you set off from'.

The trap is the boarding particle: you get on a train AT the station, so it's 출발역'에서' 타다 (action-location 에서), never 출발역을 타다 — 타다 takes the vehicle as its object (기차를 타다), while the station is just where that happens.

mistakes: Saying 출발역을 타요 — you board the train, not the station: 출발역'에서' 기차'를' 타요.
Confusing 출발역 with 도착역 — 출발역 is where you start/board, 도착역 is where you end/get off; don't swap them on a booking.
Using 출발 (the departure event) where you need the station — 'my departure station is Seoul Station' is 출발역이 서울역이에요, not 출발이 서울역이에요.

usage: get off at the arrival station
에서 + 내리다; the action of alighting happens there
this stop is the arrival station
이번 역 (this stop) is the announcement framing for 'we're here'
도착 到着 + 시각 時刻; the ETA on your ticket
all the way to the arrival station
까지 = up to; marks the trip's end point
examples: 도착역에서 내려요.
I get off at the arrival station.
simple; 에서 marks where the getting-off happens
도착역이 부산역이라서 끝까지 가요.
The arrival station is Busan Station, so I ride to the very end.
everyday; 이라서 (because it is) + 끝까지 (to the end)
이번 역이 도착역이니까 짐 챙기세요.
This stop is your arrival station, so gather your things.
real announcement tone; -니까 (since) + 챙기다 (gather/pack up)
nuance: 도착역 到着驛 stacks 到 (reach) + 着 (attach/land) + 驛 (station) = 'the station you arrive at', the endpoint of a train trip. Its mirror-image partner is 출발역 (departure station), and the pair frames every ticket. Distinguish 도착역 (the arrival STATION) from 도착 (到着, the act/fact of arriving) and from 목적지 (your overall destination, which may be reached after leaving the station): on the train itself, the stop where you alight is your 도착역. The contrast with 종착역 (終着驛, the train's final terminus) also matters — your 도착역 is where YOU get off, which may come before the line's 종착역. The English-speaker pitfall is the alighting particle: you get off AT the station, so 도착역'에서' 내리다 (action-location 에서), not 도착역을 내리다 — 내리다 is intransitive here, taking the place with 에서, not the station as an object.

The trap is the alighting particle: you get off AT the station, so 도착역'에서' 내리다 (action-location 에서), not 도착역을 내리다 — 내리다 is intransitive here, taking the place with 에서, not the station as an object.

mistakes: Saying 도착역을 내려요 — 내리다 (get off) takes the place with 에서: 도착역'에서' 내려요.
Confusing 도착역 with 출발역 — 도착역 is where you get off at the end; 출발역 is where you boarded.
Assuming 도착역 equals the line's last stop — your 도착역 is where you personally alight; the train's final terminus is 종착역.

usage: 사다 (buy); the ticket is the object with 를, verb is not 하다
book a plane ticket in advance
예매하다 豫買 = reserve-and-buy ahead, the natural word for flights/trains
왕복 往復 (going and returning) ↔ 편도 (one way)
비싸다 (expensive) describes the fare with 가/이
examples: 비행기표를 샀어요.
I bought a plane ticket.
simple past of 사다; ticket as object with 를
성수기라 비행기표가 너무 비싸요.
It's peak season, so plane tickets are way too expensive.
everyday gripe; 성수기 (high season) + 비싸다 about the fare
왕복 비행기표를 미리 예매했어요.
I booked a round-trip plane ticket in advance.
real planning; 왕복 (round trip) + 예매하다 (book ahead)
nuance: 비행기표 is a transparent compound: 비행기 飛行機 (飛 fly + 行 go + 機 machine = 'flying machine', airplane) + 표 票 (ticket) = 'plane ticket'. A common synonym is 항공권 航空券 (航空 aviation + 券 ticket/voucher), which is the formal/written term you see on booking sites and itineraries, whereas 비행기표 is the everyday spoken version — same thing, different register. The bare 표 means any ticket (train, movie, concert), so 비행기 is what specifies a flight. The verbs are 사다 (buy) and especially 예매하다 (book ahead), with 예약하다 (reserve) also fine. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 하다: 'do/get a ticket' does not translate — you 'buy' or 'book' it, so say 비행기표를 사다 / 예매하다, not 비행기표를 하다. A second trap is dropping 비행기 and saying only 표, which is too vague when a flight is meant.

structuredNuance.t: 비행기표 means 'plane ticket'. The bare 표 means any ticket (train, movie, concert), so 비행기 is what specifies a flight. The verbs are 사다 (buy) and especially 예매하다 (book ahead), with 예약하다 (reserve) also fine.

A common synonym is 항공권 航空券 (航空 aviation + 券 ticket/voucher), which is the formal/written term you see on booking sites and itineraries, whereas 비행기표 is the everyday spoken version — same thing, different register.
A transparent compound: 비행기 飛行機 (飛 fly + 行 go + 機 machine = 'flying machine', airplane) + 표 票 (ticket) = 'plane ticket'.

The trap is reaching for 하다: 'do/get a ticket' does not translate — you 'buy' or 'book' it, so say 비행기표를 사다 / 예매하다, not 비행기표를 하다. A second trap is dropping 비행기 and saying only 표, which is too vague when a flight is meant.

mistakes: Saying 비행기표를 해요 — you don't 'do' a ticket; you 비행기표를 '사요' (buy) or '예매해요' (book).
Using bare 표 for a flight — 표 alone could be any ticket; specify with 비행기표 (or 항공권) for a plane.
Treating 항공권 and 비행기표 as different things — they're the same; 항공권 is just the formal/written term you meet on booking sites.
